subjective.question: Define a power series.
subjective.answer: An infinite series of the form Σ_{n=0}^{∞} a_n (x - x_0)^n, where x_0 and a_0, a_1, a_2, ... are constants, is called a power series in (x - x_0). If x_0 = 0, the power series becomes Σ_{n=0}^{∞} a_n x^n.

subjective.question: Define a bounded sequence.
subjective.answer: A sequence {s_n} is bounded above if there is a real number b such that s_n <= b for all n, and bounded below if there is a real number a such that s_n >= a for all n. A sequence is bounded if it is both bounded above and bounded below, i.e. there exist a, b with a <= s_n <= b for all n (equivalently, |s_n| <= M for some M and all n).

subjective.question: Define supremum and infimum of a set.
subjective.answer: Let A be a set of real numbers. If b is an upper bound of A and no number less than b is an upper bound of A, then b is the supremum (least upper bound) of A, written b = sup A. If a is a lower bound of A and no number greater than a is a lower bound of A, then a is the infimum (greatest lower bound) of A, written a = inf A.

subjective.question: Define an upper bound of a set.
subjective.answer: Let A be a nonempty set of real numbers. A real number b is called an upper bound of A if x <= b for every x in A. If such a b exists, A is said to be bounded above.

subjective.question: Define the limit superior and limit inferior of a sequence {s_n}.
subjective.answer: If {s_n} is bounded above and does not diverge to -∞, there is a unique real number s* (the limit superior) such that for every ε > 0, s_n < s* + ε for all large n, and s_n > s* - ε for infinitely many n; we write s* = lim sup s_n. Similarly, if {s_n} is bounded below and does not diverge to +∞, there is a unique real number s_* (the limit inferior) such that for every ε > 0, s_n > s_* - ε for all large n, and s_n < s_* + ε for infinitely many n; we write s_* = lim inf s_n. If {s_n} is unbounded above, lim sup s_n = +∞; if it is unbounded below, lim inf s_n = -∞.

subjective.question: Define a Cauchy sequence.
subjective.answer: A sequence {s_n} of real numbers is called a Cauchy sequence if for every ε > 0 there is an integer N such that |s_n - s_m| < ε whenever m, n >= N.

subjective.question: Define an oscillatory series.
subjective.answer: A divergent series that does not diverge to +∞ or to -∞ is said to be an oscillatory series (it oscillates, finitely or infinitely).

subjective.question: Define the number e.
subjective.answer: The number e is defined by the infinite series e = Σ_{n=0}^{∞} 1/n! = 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + ..., where n! = 1.2.3...n and 0! = 1.

subjective.question: State the principle of mathematical induction.
subjective.answer: Let P(n) be a mathematical statement for n in N. If (i) P(1) is true (basis step), and (ii) P(k) being true implies P(k + 1) is true (inductive step), then P(n) is true for all n in N. Example: for P(n): 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2, P(1) gives 1 = 1.2/2 = 1, true; if P(k) holds, then 1 + ... + k + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2, so P(k + 1) holds; hence P(n) holds for all n.

subjective.question: State the ratio test.
subjective.answer: Let Σ a_n be a series of positive terms and suppose L = lim (a_{n+1}/a_n) exists. If L < 1, the series converges; if L > 1, the series diverges; if L = 1, the test is inconclusive.

subjective.question: State the Cauchy root test.
subjective.answer: Let a_n >= 0 for n >= k, and let α = lim sup a_n^{1/n}. If α < 1, then Σ a_n < ∞ (the series converges). If α > 1, then Σ a_n = ∞ (the series diverges). If α = 1, the test is inconclusive.

subjective.question: State Abel's test.
subjective.answer: Let {b_n} be a monotonic sequence that converges to 0, i.e. b_{n+1} <= b_n and lim b_n = 0 (or the same with signs reversed). If the partial sums of Σ a_n are bounded, i.e. there is M with |a_k + a_{k+1} + ... + a_n| <= M for all n >= k, then the series Σ a_n b_n converges.

subjective.question: State Dirichlet's test.
subjective.answer: If {a_n} is a nonincreasing sequence of positive terms with lim a_n = 0, and the partial sums of Σ b_n are bounded (|b_k + ... + b_n| <= M for some constant M and all n >= k), then the series Σ a_n b_n converges.

subjective.question: State the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem.
subjective.answer: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence. Equivalently, every bounded infinite set of real numbers has a limit point in R.

subjective.question: State the Cauchy convergence criterion for sequences.
subjective.answer: A sequence of real numbers is convergent if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence: for every ε > 0 there is an integer N such that |s_n - s_m| < ε for all m, n >= N. (This is the completeness of R expressed for sequences: R has no 'gaps', so a sequence whose terms eventually cluster together must have a limit in R.)

subjective.question: State the Archimedean property of R.
subjective.answer: For every real number x there exists a natural number n such that n > x. Equivalently, for any two positive real numbers x and y there is a natural number n with nx > y; the set N is not bounded above in R.

subjective.question: Prove that a convergent sequence is bounded.
subjective.answer: Let lim s_n = s. Take ε = 1. There is an integer N such that |s_n - s| < 1 for all n >= N, so |s_n| = |(s_n - s) + s| <= |s_n - s| + |s| < 1 + |s| for n >= N. Let M = max{|s_1|, |s_2|, ..., |s_{N-1}|, 1 + |s|}. Then |s_n| <= M for every n, so {s_n} is bounded.

subjective.question: Prove that √8 is an irrational number.
subjective.answer: We prove this by contradiction. Note √8 = √(4.2) = 2√2, so it is enough to recall that √2 is irrational. Suppose √2 = p/q where p, q are coprime positive integers, q != 0. Then p^2 = 2q^2, so p^2 is even, hence p is even, say p = 2r. Then 4r^2 = 2q^2, so q^2 = 2r^2, hence q is also even, contradicting that p and q are coprime. Therefore √2 is irrational, and so √8 = 2√2 is irrational (a rational multiple of an irrational number is irrational).

subjective.question: Prove that √12 is an irrational number.
subjective.answer: We prove this by contradiction. Note √12 = √(4.3) = 2√3, so it suffices to show √3 is irrational. Suppose √3 = p/q with p, q coprime positive integers. Then p^2 = 3q^2, so 3 divides p^2, hence 3 divides p; write p = 3r. Then 9r^2 = 3q^2, so q^2 = 3r^2, hence 3 divides q as well, contradicting coprimality. Therefore √3, and hence √12 = 2√3, is irrational.

subjective.question: Prove by mathematical induction that n < 3^n for all n in N.
subjective.answer: For n = 1: 1 < 3^1 = 3, so the statement holds. Suppose n < 3^n for some n >= 1. Then n + 1 <= 2n (since n >= 1), and 2n < 2.3^n (by the induction hypothesis), and 2.3^n < 3.3^n = 3^{n+1}. Hence n + 1 < 3^{n+1}, so the statement holds for n + 1. By induction, n < 3^n for all n in N.

subjective.question: Show that if {s_n} is nondecreasing and bounded above, then lim s_n = sup {s_n}.
subjective.answer: Let s = sup {s_n : n in N}, which exists by the completeness axiom since {s_n} is bounded above. Let ε > 0. Since s - ε is not an upper bound, there is N with s_N > s - ε. As {s_n} is nondecreasing, for all n >= N, s - ε < s_N <= s_n <= s < s + ε, i.e. |s_n - s| < ε. Hence lim s_n = s = sup {s_n}.

subjective.question: Prove that e = lim (1 + 1/n)^n.
subjective.answer: Let s_n = (1 + 1/n)^n. By the binomial theorem, s_n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k) (1/n)^k = Σ_{k=0}^{n} (1/k!) . n(n - 1)...(n - k + 1)/n^k = Σ_{k=0}^{n} (1/k!)(1)(1 - 1/n)...(1 - (k - 1)/n). Each term increases with n and there are more terms as n grows, so {s_n} is increasing. Also each factor (1 - j/n) < 1, so s_n <= Σ_{k=0}^{n} 1/k! <= Σ_{k=0}^{∞} 1/k! = e; hence {s_n} is bounded above. Therefore lim s_n exists, and comparing the expansions term by term gives lim s_n = Σ_{k=0}^{∞} 1/k! = e.

subjective.question: Give an approximation of the number e.
subjective.answer: By definition e = Σ_{n=0}^{∞} 1/n! = 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + ... . The partial sums give S_0 = 1, S_1 = 2, S_2 = 2.5, S_3 ≈ 2.6667, S_4 ≈ 2.7083, S_5 ≈ 2.7167, S_6 ≈ 2.7181, increasing to e. Since the remainder after n terms is less than 1/(n.n!), e is approximated as e ≈ 2.71828; in particular 2 < e < 3.

subjective.question: Show that the Cauchy root test is inconclusive for the series Σ 1/n^p.
subjective.answer: Here a_n = 1/n^p, so a_n^{1/n} = (1/n^p)^{1/n} = exp(-(p/n) log n). Since (log n)/n -> 0, lim a_n^{1/n} = e^0 = 1 for every p. Thus lim sup a_n^{1/n} = 1, the inconclusive case of the root test, for all p; yet Σ 1/n^p converges for p > 1 and diverges for p <= 1, which shows the test really gives no information when the limit is 1.

subjective.question: Test the series Σ (-1)^n n!
subjective.answer: / (α(α + 1)...(α + n - 1)), α > 0, for absolute convergence. (Raabe's test) Apply Raabe's test to b_n = n! / (α(α + 1)...(α + n - 1)) > 0. We have b_n / b_{n+1} = (α + n)/(n + 1), so n(b_n/b_{n+1} - 1) = n(α + n - (n + 1))/(n + 1) = n(α - 1)/(n + 1) -> α - 1. By Raabe's test, Σ b_n converges if α - 1 > 1, i.e. α > 2, and diverges if α - 1 < 1, i.e. α < 2. Hence the given series converges absolutely if α > 2 and does not converge absolutely if α < 2.

subjective.question: Discuss whether the sequence {n/2 + 1/n} converges or diverges.
subjective.answer: The sequence diverges to +∞. Indeed, if a is any real number, then n/2 + 1/n > a whenever n >= 2a (since n/2 >= a and 1/n > 0). Therefore lim (n/2 + 1/n) = +∞, so the sequence is divergent (unbounded).

subjective.question: Discuss whether the sequence {n - n^2} converges or diverges.
subjective.answer: The sequence diverges to -∞. Write n - n^2 = -n(n - 1). If a is any real number, then -n(n - 1) < a whenever n > 1 + √|a|. Therefore lim (n - n^2) = -∞, so the sequence is divergent (unbounded below).

subjective.question: Find the limit of the sequence s_n = (1/n) sin(nπ/4) + 2(1 + 3/n)/(1 + 1/n).
subjective.answer: lim s_n = lim (1/n) sin(nπ/4) + 2(1 + 3/n)/(1 + 1/n). The first term tends to 0 because |(1/n) sin(nπ/4)| <= 1/n -> 0. The second term tends to 2(1 + 0)/(1 + 0) = 2. Hence lim s_n = 0 + 2 = 2.

subjective.question: Find lim (n/2 + log n) / (3n + 4√n).
subjective.answer: Divide numerator and denominator by n: (n/2 + log n)/(3n + 4√n) = (1/2 + (log n)/n) / (3 + 4/√n). Since (log n)/n -> 0 and 4/√n -> 0, the limit is (1/2 + 0)/(3 + 0) = 1/6.

subjective.question: If S = {x : x >= -2}, find sup S and inf S.
subjective.answer: Every element of S is >= -2 and -2 itself belongs to S, so inf S = -2 (the greatest lower bound, attained). S is not bounded above, since x can be arbitrarily large; hence S has no supremum in R (one writes sup S = +∞ in the extended real number system).

subjective.question: Find an open cover of S = [0, 1].
subjective.answer: For each n in N let U_n = (-1/n, 1 + 1/n), an open interval. Every x in [0, 1] satisfies -1/n < x < 1 + 1/n, so x in U_n; hence [0, 1] ⊂ ∪_{n=1}^{∞} U_n, i.e. {U_n : n in N} is an open cover of [0, 1]. (Indeed, the single open interval (-1, 2) alone is already an open cover.)

subjective.question: Give an example of a sequence that does not converge but has a convergent subsequence.
subjective.answer: Take s_n = (-1)^n. The sequence itself does not converge (it oscillates between -1 and 1, and lim inf s_n = -1 != 1 = lim sup s_n). But its subsequence of even terms, s_{2n} = 1, converges to 1, and the subsequence of odd terms converges to -1.

subjective.question: For the power series Σ [sin(nπ/6) / 2^n] (x - 1)^n, find a_n, x_0 and the radius of convergence R.
subjective.answer: Comparing with Σ a_n (x - x_0)^n gives a_n = sin(nπ/6)/2^n and x_0 = 1. By the root test, lim sup |a_n|^{1/n} = (1/2) . lim sup |sin(nπ/6)|^{1/n} = 1/2 (since |sin(nπ/6)| <= 1 and the values arbitrarily close to 1 occur). Hence R = 1/(1/2) = 2.

subjective.question: Determine the radius of convergence of the power series Σ x^n / n!.
subjective.answer: Here a_n = 1/n!. By the ratio test, |a_{n+1}/a_n| = n!/(n + 1)! = 1/(n + 1) -> 0. Hence R = ∞: the series converges for every real x.

subjective.question: Find the radius of convergence of the power series Σ n!
subjective.answer: x^n. Here a_n = n!. By the ratio test, |a_{n+1}/a_n| = (n + 1)!/n! = n + 1 -> ∞. Hence R = 0: the series converges only at x = 0.

subjective.question: Write any one subsequence of the sequence {1/n^2}.
subjective.answer: Taking only the terms with even index, n = 2k, gives the subsequence {1/(2k)^2} = {1/(4k^2)}: 1/4, 1/16, 1/36, 1/64, ... . (Any choice of terms with strictly increasing indices is a subsequence, e.g. the terms at indices 1, 4, 9, 16, ... give 1, 1/16, 1/81, 1/256, ... .)
